metadata.title: AI vs. the Data Deluge
metadata.purpose: Weekly STEM explainer Ep.01: how AI triage (AstroNet, Kepler-90i, Rubin Observatory) finds signals in more data than any human team could review by hand. beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about how AI helps astronomers find real signals hidden inside far more data than any human team could ever check by hand.

shot.note: NEW 2026-08-01. Presenter self-introduction / executive summary card, inserted as beat 2 right after the cold open. Not a factual claim beat — see FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: In 2017, a computer found a planet every human who'd looked at the data had missed.

shot.note: Abstract field of data points/light curves, one quietly highlighted — no literal computer/planet imagery.

beats.narration_text: Not because the data was hidden — because there was too much of it to check by hand.

props.headline: Not hidden — just too much to check by hand.

beats.narration_text: Kepler stared at up to 200000 stars for four years, recording brightness every 30 minutes — millions of light curves.
A transiting planet leaves one signature: a tiny, periodic dip in a star's brightness.

shot.note: Animated transit dip on a single light curve.

beats.narration_text: Pipelines flagged thousands of candidates. Sorting real transits from noise took time nobody had.

props.headline: Thousands of candidates. Sorting them took time nobody had.

shot.note: Tightened 2026-07-26 (was 21 words) to make room for the new architecture beats. UI dashboard mockup — flagged signals scrolling, marked candidate vs. noise.

beats.narration_text: So how do you find the one signal nobody ever had time to check?

props.headline: So how do you find the one signal nobody ever had time to check?

beats.narration_text: In 2017, Google engineer Christopher Shallue and astronomer Andrew Vanderburg tried something different.

props.headline: Christopher Shallue & Andrew Vanderburg tried something different.

beats.narration_text: They trained a neural network on 15000 light curves humans had already labeled by hand.
The network didn't look at one curve — it compared two views: the full orbit, and a close-up of just the dip.

shot.note: NEW 2026-07-26. Split-screen: wide folded light curve (global view, left/top) next to a zoomed dip (local view, right/bottom) — visually sets up beat 10's payoff.

beats.narration_text: The wide view exposes impostors — like a second eclipse revealing two stars, not one planet. The close-up checks the dip's shape.

shot.note: NEW 2026-07-26. Two side-by-side examples: a real transit (clean single dip, both views agree) vs. an eclipsing binary (extra dip visible only in the wide/global view).

beats.narration_text: Only then did it decide: a real planet, or just another false alarm.

shot.note: Synthesis beat — the two views merging into one output. Replaces the old, more generic 'network learned what a transit looks like' line.

beats.narration_text: It flagged Kepler-90i — with only a 1-in-10000 chance of being a false alarm.

shot.note: Light curve highlight/zoom on the flagged dip.

beats.narration_text: That made Kepler-90 the first known system with eight planets outside our own.

shot.note: NASA/Ames official artist concept, image PIA22193.

beats.narration_text: Overall, the network told real planets from false alarms correctly 96% of the time.

props.headline: 96% accuracy — real planets vs. false alarms

beats.narration_text: This same idea now runs continuously — Vera Rubin Observatory alone produces about 10 terabytes of images every night.
That's up to seven million alerts a night, across a ten-year survey expected to total roughly 60 petabytes.

props.headline: Up to 7,000,000 alerts / night — ~60 petabytes over 10 years

beats.narration_text: No human team could review that. The universe was never short on signals — just on hours.

shot.note: Tightened 2026-07-26 (was 22 words). NOIRLab 'Zooming into NSF-DOE Rubin's Ocean of Stars' HD video — same archive asset as before, new (shorter) narration.

beats.narration_text: AI doesn't replace the astronomer looking through the telescope. It decides what's worth their time.

props.headline: AI doesn't replace the astronomer. It decides what's worth their time.
